items.name: Human Biology -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
The prevailing medical doctrine of the period attributed peptic ulcers to psychological stress and excess gastric acid. In 1979, at Royal Perth Hospital, Robin Warren observed curved bacilli in gastric biopsy specimens. Resolving which account was correct required the organism to be cultured, characterised and placed within bacterial taxonomy, work that occupied the first years of the inquiry. The bacterium was initially given the name Campylobacter pyloridis. As a separate matter of record, the organism was reclassified into the new genus Helicobacter in 1989.

Physiology then explained how such an organism survives where no ordinary bacterium can. H. pylori secretes urease, which hydrolyses urea and buffers the surrounding gastric acid; this enzymatic activity gave rise to the urea breath test used to diagnose infection. The results of that test confirm that H. pylori infection is present in the large majority of patients with duodenal ulcers. For any single ulcer, at least one of two exposures is operative, and in a proportion of patients both together: colonisation by the organism, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug exposure, which accounts for most peptic ulcers in patients without H. pylori infection.

Prevalence alone does not establish causation, since a widespread organism can inhabit a diseased stomach without producing the disease. The decisive argument came instead from the behaviour of the lesion under treatment directed at acid and at the bacterium respectively. Ulcer recurrence within one year exceeded 50% in patients treated with acid suppression alone. The clinical maxim "no acid, no ulcer" summarised the pre-1980s understanding of ulcer causation. By contrast, antibiotic eradication left annual ulcer recurrence at approximately 60% of treated patients.

Eliminating the bacterium with antibiotics permanently cured ulcer disease in most patients, and the persistence of relapse in some six of every ten treated patients cannot be squared with such a permanent cure; the two descriptions of post-eradication outcome cannot both be true. Put differently, antimicrobial eradication of H. pylori produced durable remission of peptic ulceration in the majority of treated patients. Because that durable remission demonstrated that removing the organism removes the disease, the Nobel Prize for the discovery of H. pylori was awarded in 1995. Ulcer disease was thereafter managed as an infection, with acid suppression retained as an adjunct to mucosal healing rather than as treatment of the underlying cause.
